parts.label: (a)(i)
key_concepts: Fleming left-hand rule with electron flow
hints: Hint 1: Picture the two directions you know - the electrons are moving into the slice and $B$ points to the right. Remember conventional current is opposite to electron flow when you apply the left-hand rule.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Sort out velocity and field directions**
Think of an electron entering face PQKJ and moving through the slice. Its velocity $v$ is into the slice, while magnetic flux density $B$ points to the right across the slice. They are perpendicular, so there is a maximum magnetic force $F = Bqv$.

Step 2: **Apply the left-hand rule carefully**
For negative charges, it helps to first find the direction for a positive charge moving the same way, then reverse it. Using Fleming's left-hand rule, First finger along $B$ to the right, Second finger along conventional current (opposite to electron motion, so out of the slice), your thumb points upwards for positive charge. Reverse this for electrons, giving a force downwards.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Follow where the electrons from (a)(i) will pile up. The face they are pushed towards becomes negative and the opposite face is left positive.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **See where charge builds up**
The magnetic force pushes all the free electrons downwards as they drift through. So electrons accumulate on the bottom face and leave a deficit of electrons (positive charge) on the top face.

Step 2: **Name the faces**
Looking at Fig. 8.1, the top face is PQRS and the bottom face is JKLM. The separation of charge between these two faces is what creates the Hall p.d.

parts.label: (b)
key_concepts: balance of electric and magnetic forces
hints: Hint 1: Think about what a separation of positive and negative charge on opposite faces must create in the space between them.
Hint 2: Think about the two forces now acting on a moving electron in the slice and what happens when they become equal in size but opposite in direction.
parts.proper_answer: Separated charge sets up a transverse electric field (and p.d.). This exerts an upward electric force on electrons opposite to the downward magnetic force. Maximum is reached when electric force equals magnetic force, so no further net transverse deflection and charge separation stops.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **A second field appears**
Once electrons pile up on one face, you have negative charge on the bottom and positive on the top. Opposite charges attract, so an electric field $E$ is set up from top to bottom across the slice. This field grows as more charge separates.

Step 2: **Two opposing forces compete**
Every new electron moving through now feels two transverse forces: downward magnetic force $F_B = Bqv$ and upward electric force $F_E = Eq$. At first $F_B$ wins and more separation happens, but as $E$ grows, $F_E$ grows too.

Step 3: **Equilibrium gives maximum p.d.**
Soon $$F_E = F_B$$ $$Eq = Bqv$$ At that point there is no net transverse force, electrons go straight through with no further deflection, and the charge and p.d. stop increasing. That steady value is the maximum Hall voltage.

parts.label: (c)
hints: Hint 1: Focus on the thickness that separates the two Hall faces. Convert PQ = 0.10 mm into metres and list $B$, $I$ and $n$ with SI units.
Hint 2: Recall how Hall voltage links $B$, $I$, carrier density $n$, thickness $t$ and elementary charge $q$, then substitute carefully with powers of ten.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Choose the correct Hall relation**
At equilibrium, $E = Bv$ and $E = V_H/d$ where $d$ is the separation of the Hall faces. Combined with $I = nAvq$ this gives the familiar form: $$V_H = \frac{BI}{ntq}$$ Here $t$ is the thickness PQ perpendicular to both $B$ and $I$, $n = 1.3 \times 10^{29} \text{ m}^{-3}$, $q = 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$.

Step 2: **Convert and substitute**
$$t = 0.10 \text{ mm} = 1.0 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}$$ $$B = 4.6 \times 10^{-3} \text{ T}, \quad I = 6.3 \times 10^{-4} \text{ A}$$ $$V_H = \frac{(4.6 \times 10^{-3})(6.3 \times 10^{-4})}{(1.3 \times 10^{29})(1.0 \times 10^{-4})(1.60 \times 10^{-19})}$$

Step 3: **Calculate**
Numerator $= 2.90 \times 10^{-6}$. Denominator $= 2.08 \times 10^{6}$. $$V_H = 1.4 \times 10^{-12} \text{ V}$$ This tiny value is typical for a metal with huge $n$.

parts.label: (d)
key_concepts: carrier density in semiconductors vs metals
inverse dependence of Hall voltage on n
hints: Hint 1: Look at your answer to (c) - it is about $10^{-12}$ V. Ask yourself what in the formula $V_H = BI/ntq$ makes it so small for a metal.
Hint 2: Compare the number of free charge carriers per cubic metre in a semiconductor with that in a metal, and work out what that does to $V_H$.
parts.proper_answer: Semiconductors have a much smaller number density $n$ of free charge carriers than metals. Since $V_H$ is proportional to $1/n$, the Hall voltage is much larger and easier to measure.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot why the metal signal is tiny**
Your value in (c), about $10^{-12}$ V, is far too small to measure reliably. From $$V_H = \frac{BI}{ntq}$$ you can see $V_H$ is inversely proportional to $n$. Metals have an enormous $n \approx 10^{28}$ to $10^{29} \text{ m}^{-3}$, so $V_H$ is crushed.

Step 2: **Why semiconductors help**
A semiconductor has far fewer free carriers per unit volume, typically many orders of magnitude smaller $n$. A smaller denominator gives a much larger $V_H$ for the same $B$ and $I$, so the probe is sensitive enough to detect and measure magnetic fields practically.
